prompt: What is compliance, in this lesson's terms?

choices.text: Meeting others' requirements, provably
choices.why: Right. A law, a regulation, a contract or a chosen standard.

choices.text: Being protected against the risks that matter
choices.why: That is security.

choices.text: Having no incidents during the year
choices.why: Compliant organisations have incidents too.

choices.text: Buying the products an auditor recommends
choices.why: Auditors check controls; they do not sell them.

prompt: A company ticks every box on its checklist and is breached through something the checklist never asked about. Which box of the lesson's table is it in?

choices.text: Neither secure nor compliant
choices.why: Every box was ticked.

choices.text: Compliant and not secure
choices.why: Right. Checkbox security.

choices.text: Secure and not compliant
choices.why: It met the checklist; it lacked the security.

choices.text: Secure and compliant
choices.why: It was breached.

prompt: ana protects the shop well and has written nothing down. What does the lesson say about that?

choices.text: It is the ideal: security without paperwork
choices.why: Unproven protection cannot be told apart from none.

choices.text: Unproven, it looks like no protection at all
choices.why: Right. To a customer, an auditor or the ANPD.

choices.text: Auditors accept a verbal description instead
choices.why: Inquiry is the weakest evidence.

choices.text: It means the shop is not secure
choices.why: It may be secure; it cannot show it.

prompt: Match each requirement to its kind of source.

pairs.left: PCI DSS, through the payment provider
ISO 27001, chosen for a large customer

prompt: How did the shop shrink its PCI DSS obligations to a short questionnaire?

choices.text: Card numbers never touch its server
choices.why: Right. Customers pay on the provider's page.

choices.text: By encrypting card numbers on its own server
choices.why: That still means storing them, which keeps the full scope.

choices.text: By asking the card brands for an exemption
choices.why: No such exemption is described.

choices.text: By getting ISO 27001 certified first
choices.why: One standard does not replace the other.

prompt: Order the chain an auditor follows backwards, from the start.
hint: From what is required to what proves it.
trap: A policy answers the requirement, a procedure carries the policy out, and evidence shows it was done.

prompt: Why does the lesson recommend a control mapping?

choices.text: It replaces the need for evidence
choices.why: Each control still needs its evidence.

choices.text: Do the work once, show it many times
choices.why: Right. An access review answers the LGPD, PCI DSS and ISO 27001.

choices.text: So every requirement gets its own separate control
choices.why: The point is the opposite: one control, many requirements.

choices.text: Auditors forbid controls that serve two standards
choices.why: They accept it; it is common.

prompt: Order these kinds of evidence from weakest to strongest.
trap: Each step relies less on what somebody says and more on what the auditor sees.

prompt: Three of twenty-five sampled accounts belong to people who left months ago. The access policy reads well. What does the auditor conclude?

choices.text: The control has failed
choices.why: Right. It must work every time, not only in the cases expected to be looked at.

choices.text: Nothing, since a sample proves nothing
choices.why: Sampling is how audits reach conclusions.

choices.text: Only those three accounts need fixing
choices.why: The process that let them happen is the finding.

choices.text: The control works, since the policy is sound
choices.why: A policy is intent; the sample is practice.

prompt: What makes evidence good, in the lesson's three words?

choices.text: Dated, attributable and kept
choices.why: Right. A log entry beats an email saying done.

choices.text: Recent, short and verbal
choices.why: Verbal is the weakest kind.

choices.text: Encrypted, hidden and backed up
choices.why: Hidden evidence helps nobody.

choices.text: Long, signed and printed
choices.why: Length and paper are not the criteria.

prompt: Why does the lesson say the shop's first audit will mostly consist of opening files?
hint: Look back at the earlier lessons.

choices.text: The earlier lessons already produced the records
choices.why: Right. Evidence as a side effect of doing the work.

choices.text: Because auditors only read files and never interview anyone
choices.why: They interview too.

choices.text: Because the files were written for the auditor
choices.why: None of them was; that is the point.

choices.text: Because the shop is too small to audit properly
choices.why: Size is not the reason.

prompt: Match each finding to its grade.
hint: Not at all, partly, not yet.

pairs.left: no access review has ever been done
two of twenty-five sampled accounts belonged to leavers
nothing is wrong, but the auditor sees a risk

prompt: What makes an internal audit independent?

choices.text: It uses only automated tools
choices.why: Tools are not what makes it independent.

choices.text: Auditors who don't run that area
choices.why: Right. Nobody checks their own work.

choices.text: It is kept secret from management
choices.why: Its findings go to management.

choices.text: It is done by an outside company
choices.why: That is an external audit.

prompt: ana knows of a gap the auditor has not found. What does the lesson advise?

choices.text: Ask the auditor to skip that area
choices.why: The scope is agreed at planning, not negotiated away.

choices.text: Tell the auditor, with a plan
choices.why: Right. That reads as the organisation managing its own risks.

choices.text: Say nothing unless asked directly
choices.why: A concealed problem, once found, costs all trust.

choices.text: Fix it quietly during the audit
choices.why: Telling it, with a plan, is better.

prompt: Match each line to what it does.

pairs.right: owns the risks and runs the controls
sets the framework, monitors and challenges
gives independent assurance to the governing body

prompt: Who sits above the three lines and sets the risk appetite?

choices.text: The regulator
choices.why: Regulators are outside the organisation.

choices.text: The governing body
choices.why: Right. The board, or the owners.

choices.text: The IT team
choices.why: IT is in the first line.

choices.text: The external auditor
choices.why: External auditors sit outside.

prompt: ana configured the firewall and is asked to audit it too. Which lesson 4 idea does the Three Lines Model apply here?
hint: Her blind spots would be in both places.

choices.text: Two layers that share a cause are one
choices.why: Right. The same person doing and checking.

choices.text: Prevention matters more than detection
choices.why: The lesson said neither alone is enough.

choices.text: Defence in depth needs at least seven layers
choices.why: No such number is required.

choices.text: Compensating controls need a date
choices.why: True, and not the idea at stake here.

prompt: Which of these are good audit evidence for the shop's access reviews? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: an email reading "done" with no list attached
choices.why: Says nothing about what was reviewed.

choices.text: last September's review, signed by bruno
choices.why: Dated and attributable.

choices.text: ana saying the reviews are always done
choices.why: Inquiry: the weakest kind.

choices.text: the log of accounts removed after the review, with dates
choices.why: Shows the review had an effect.
